pos: n., v. (a concealed force; rendering Hebrew arab)
etymology: From Old French embuscher, to hide in the woods. An ambush is a force that exists before it is seen.
biblical_def: An ambush is a hidden force set to strike. Joshua's taking of Ai turns on one: “And Joshua rose up… and chose out thirty thousand mighty men of valour, and sent them away by night… lie in wait against the city, even behind the city” (Jos 8:3–4). Jehoshaphat's victory reverses the picture — the LORD set ambushments against the enemy while Judah merely sang (2Ch 20:22). Jeremiah warns Israel that God Himself may become the hidden adversary, and Proverbs warns the young man that sinners lay wait for their own blood (Pro 1:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ambush as a private or concealed station where troops lie in wait to attack by surprise; and the troops so posted.
webster_full: AMBUSH, n. A private or concealed station, where troops lie in wait to attack their enemy by surprise.
2. The troops posted in a concealed place, for attacking by surprise.
3. A lying in wait, for the purpose of attacking by surprise.
scriptures: Jos 8:4
And he commanded them, saying, Behold, ye shall lie in wait against the city, even behind the city: go not very far from the city, but be ye all ready:
And when they began to sing and to praise, the LORD set ambushments against the children of Ammon, Moab, and mount Seir, which were come against Judah; and they were smitten. And
Pro 1:18
And they lay wait for their own blood; they lurk privily for their own lives.
Jdg 9:34
And Abimelech rose up, and all the people that were with him, by night, and they laid wait against Shechem in four companies.
corruption_summary: Spiritual danger is imagined as a frontal assault, so believers watch the road ahead and are taken from the side — which is the only way an ambush ever works.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Chronicles 20:22 is the passage worth memorizing, because the ambush belongs to God: when they began to sing and to praise, the LORD set ambushments against the children of Ammon, Moab, and mount Seir. Judah's contribution was worship; the concealed force was the LORD's. Believers facing odds they cannot compute are not told to devise cleverness but to praise, on the understanding that the field contains forces they cannot see.

Proverbs 1 applies the figure to sin's self-defeat: they lay wait for their own blood; they lurk privily for their own lives. The ambush the wicked set is, in the long providence of God, the trap they fall into. That does not make vigilance unnecessary, but it does mean the believer is never facing an enemy whose schemes are outside God's government.
roots_summary: Hebrew arab (H693), to lie in wait; the noun maarab (H3993), an ambush — the vocabulary of Joshua 8 and Judges 9.
roots_lines: Hebrew arab (H693) — to lie in wait, ambush; Joshua 8:4, Judges 9:34, Proverbs 1:11.
Hebrew maarab (H3993) — ambush, lying in wait; Joshua 8:9, 2 Chronicles 13:13.
Greek enedra (G1747) — ambush, plot; Acts 23:16 and 25:3, the plot against Paul.
usage: “Lie in wait against the city, even behind the city” — the taking of Ai.
“The LORD set ambushments” — while Judah sang.
“They lay wait for their own blood” — the trap that catches its maker.

etymology: From Latin arcus, a bow. The archer is the ancient world's distance weapon — the man who wounds without closing.
biblical_def: Archers are bowmen. Scripture notes them chiefly at the moments they wound the anointed: “the archers hit him; and he was sore wounded of the archers” (1Sa 31:3), Saul's end on Gilboa; and “the archers shot at king Josiah” (2Ch 35:23). Jacob's blessing on Joseph makes the archer a figure of slander endured: “The archers have sorely grieved him, and shot at him, and hated him: but his bow abode in strength” (Gen 49:23–24). Ishmael grows up to become an archer in the wilderness (Gen 21:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an archer as one who uses a bow; a bowman; and archery as the practice, art or skill of shooting with a bow and arrow.
webster_full: ARCHER, n. One who uses a bow; a bowman.
ARCHERY, n. The use of the bow and arrow; the practice, art or skill of archers; the act of shooting with a bow and arrow.
scriptures: And the battle went sore against Saul, and the archers hit him; and he was sore wounded of the archers. and the
The archers have sorely grieved him, and shot at him, and hated him:
But his bow abode in strength, and the arms of his hands were made strong by the hands of the mighty God of Jacob; (from thence is the shepherd, the stone of Israel:)
And the archers shot at king Josiah; and the king said to his servants, Have me away; for I am sore wounded.
corruption_summary: Attack is imagined as confrontation, when the biblical archer is precisely the enemy who never comes close — the anonymous shot from distance, which is now most of public speech.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 49:23-24 is the passage a slandered believer should keep. The archers have sorely grieved him, and shot at him, and hated him: but his bow abode in strength, and the arms of his hands were made strong by the hands of the mighty God of Jacob. Joseph is not described as unwounded — sorely grieved is granted — but as strengthened at the hands, the very place a bowman needs strength. God's answer to distance-attack was not to end it but to hold Joseph's arms steady through it.

The archer is the perfect emblem of the anonymous accusation: he strikes from beyond the range of relationship, risks nothing, and need never see the wound. Saul fell to archers, Josiah fell to archers, and Ahab was killed by an arrow shot at a venture (1Ki 22:34). Scripture's realism here is worth noting — the shot that ends a reign is often nobody's aimed masterpiece, merely an arrow loosed at random into a providence.
roots_summary: Hebrew qesheth (H7198), a bow; rabab (H7232), to shoot; the archers of Genesis 49 are literally baale chitstsim, masters of arrows.
roots_lines: Hebrew qesheth (H7198) — bow; Genesis 49:24, his bow abode in strength.
Hebrew rabab (H7232) — to shoot arrows; Genesis 49:23, the archers have sorely grieved him.
Hebrew chets (H2671) — arrow; Psalm 64:3, who bend their bows to shoot their arrows, even bitter words.
usage: “The archers hit him; and he was sore wounded” — the end of Saul on Gilboa.
“His bow abode in strength” — Joseph strengthened at the hands.
“A certain man drew a bow at a venture” — the random arrow that ends a reign.

pos: n. (a store of weapons; rendering Hebrew talpiyoth and otsar)
etymology: From Latin armatura, armour. An armoury is not a battlefield but a storehouse — strength kept ready before it is needed.
biblical_def: An armoury is a weapons store. The Song uses it as an image of the bride's beauty: “Thy neck is like the tower of David builded for an armoury, whereon there hang a thousand bucklers, all shields of mighty men” (Son 4:4). Nehemiah stations the returning builders by one (Neh 3:19), and Jeremiah announces that the LORD “hath opened his armoury, and hath brought forth the weapons of his indignation” (Jer 50:25) — God keeps an arsenal, and judgment is its issue.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines armory as a repository of arms; a place where arms and instruments of war are deposited for safe keeping.
webster_full: ARMORY, n. A repository of arms; a place where arms and instruments of war are deposited for safe keeping.
2. Armor; defensive arms.
3. Ensigns armorial.
scriptures: Son 4:4
Thy neck is like the tower of David builded for an armoury, whereon there hang a thousand bucklers, all shields of mighty men.
The LORD hath opened his armoury, and hath brought forth the weapons of his indignation: for this is the work of the Lord GOD of hosts in the land of the Chaldeans.
Neh 3:19
And next to him repaired Ezer the son of Jeshua, the ruler of Mizpah, another piece over against the going up to the armoury at the turning of the wall.
Isa 22:8
And he discovered the covering of Judah, and thou didst look in that day to the armour of the house of the forest.
corruption_summary: Christians reach for weapons at the moment of attack, having stored none — and a faith with no armoury is defenceless precisely when it needs to be armed.
corruption_paragraphs: An armoury is a doctrine about time. Weapons are gathered in peace and hung on the wall long before the day they are wanted, which is why Nehemiah's builders repaired the wall over against the armoury at the turning of the wall. The believer's equivalent is scripture memorized, doctrine understood, and habits formed while nothing is burning — because the hour of temptation is not the hour to begin acquiring resources.

Jeremiah 50:25 keeps the figure from becoming merely self-help. The LORD hath opened his armoury, and hath brought forth the weapons of his indignation: for this is the work of the Lord GOD of hosts in the land of the Chaldeans. God's own arsenal is stocked, and history's judgments are its issue. The nations that imagine no weapon exists against them have simply never seen the door of that storehouse opened.
roots_summary: Hebrew talpiyoth (H8530), armoury or arsenal, in Song 4:4; otsar (H214), a treasury or store — Jeremiah 50:25 uses it of God's own.
roots_lines: Hebrew talpiyoth (H8530) — armoury; only Song of Solomon 4:4, the tower of David.
Hebrew otsar (H214) — storehouse, treasury, armoury; Jeremiah 50:25.
Hebrew nesheq (H5402) — weapons, armour; Nehemiah 3:19, over against the going up to the armoury.
usage: “The tower of David builded for an armoury” — beauty pictured as a hung arsenal.
“The LORD hath opened his armoury” — judgment issued from God's own store.
“Over against the armoury” — builders stationed where the weapons were.

pos: n. (one who fights for another; rendering Hebrew ish habbenayim, the man between)
etymology: From Latin campio, a fighter in the field. The Hebrew is more exact: the man of the space between the armies — a representative.
biblical_def: A champion fights as his people's representative. Goliath is the Bible's example, and the Hebrew names his office precisely: “there went out a champion out of the camp of the Philistines, named Goliath” (1Sa 17:4) — literally the man between the two armies. His proposal is representative warfare: “if he be able to fight with me, and to kill me, then will we be your servants” (1Sa 17:9). The whole nation's fate hangs on one man's outcome, which is why David's victory is Israel's, and why the pattern preaches Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a champion as a man who undertakes a combat in the place or cause of another; and one who fights in his own cause, a hero.
webster_full: CHAMPION, n. A man who undertakes a combat in the place or cause of another.
2. A man who fights in his own cause.
3. A hero; a brave warrior.
CHAMPION, v.t. To challenge to a combat.
scriptures: And there went out a champion out of the camp of the Philistines, named Goliath, of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span.
If he be able to fight with me, and to kill me, then will we be your servants: but if I prevail against him, and kill him, then shall ye be our servants, and serve us.
And all this assembly shall know that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the LORD'S, and he will give you into our hands.
Rom 5:19
For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.
corruption_summary: David and Goliath is preached as a motivational story about facing giants, which reverses it — the hearer is meant to be the terrified army, not the champion.
corruption_paragraphs: The structure of 1 Samuel 17 is representative, not exemplary. Israel is not asked to be brave; Israel is asked to have a champion, and the entire nation stands or falls on his single combat. When the sermon makes the listener into David and his problems into Goliath, it has quietly replaced substitution with self-improvement — and left the trembling man in the trench with a giant and some encouragement.

Read the other way, the chapter preaches. One representative goes out on behalf of a people who cannot fight, defeats the enemy alone, and his victory is credited to everyone in the camp who did nothing but watch. That is precisely Romans 5:19 — by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. David's own confession names the ground: the battle is the LORD's, and he will give you into our hands.
roots_summary: Hebrew ish habbenayim, the man of the between-space — a representative combatant; Greek has no exact term, but the theology reappears in the one man of Romans 5.
roots_lines: Hebrew benayim (H1143) — the space between; 1 Samuel 17:4, 23, the man between the armies.
Hebrew gibbor (H1368) — mighty man, warrior; the general word for a champion in battle.
Greek heis — one; Romans 5:19's insistence that one man's act determines many.
usage: “There went out a champion out of the camp of the Philistines” — the man between the armies.
“Then will we be your servants” — the nation's fate on one combat.
“The battle is the LORD's” — the champion's own confession.

pos: n. (a light spear or missile; rendering Hebrew shebet, Greek belos)
etymology: From Old French dart, a javelin. A dart is thrown rather than thrust — a weapon that arrives before its thrower.
biblical_def: A dart is a thrown missile. Joab takes three and thrusts them through Absalom's heart (2Sa 18:14). Paul makes the word a spiritual category: “above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked” (Eph 6:16) — the ancient fire-arrow, wrapped in pitch and lit, which the leather-covered shield was soaked to extinguish. Proverbs warns of the young man going after the strange woman “till a dart strike through his liver” (Pro 7:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a dart as a pointed missile weapon to be thrown by the hand; a short lance; and any missile weapon.
webster_full: DART, n. A pointed missile weapon to be thrown by the hand; a short lance.
2. Any missile weapon.
DART, v.t. To throw a pointed instrument with a sudden thrust.
scriptures: Eph 6:16
Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked.
Then said Joab, I may not tarry thus with thee. And he took three darts in his hand, and thrust them through the heart of Absalom, while he was yet alive in the midst of the oak.
Pro 7:23
Till a dart strike through his liver; as a bird hasteth to the snare, and knoweth not that it is for his life.
The sword of him that layeth at him cannot hold: the spear, the dart, nor the habergeon.
corruption_summary: Temptation is pictured as a slow argument the believer reasons through, when Paul describes it as incoming fire requiring a shield already raised.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 6:16 rewards knowing the hardware. A fiery dart was an arrow wrapped in tow and pitch, lit and loosed, designed to set fire to whatever it struck. The Roman scutum was covered in leather and soaked before battle precisely so that such an arrow would lodge and go out. Faith functions the same way: it does not argue with the accusation mid-air, it absorbs and extinguishes it, and it must be soaked beforehand.

The word all in the verse is the pastoral comfort. Ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked — not most, not the mild ones. There is no incoming accusation, blasphemous thought, or sudden lust that faith in Christ cannot put out, which means a believer's real problem is never an unquenchable dart but a shield left on the ground.
roots_summary: Greek belos (G956), a missile, dart; Hebrew shebet (H7626), rod or dart, in 2 Samuel 18:14; chets (H2671), arrow.
roots_lines: Greek belos (G956) — a missile, dart; only Ephesians 6:16, the fiery darts of the wicked.
Greek puroo (G4448) — to set on fire; the adjective describing those darts as fiery.
Hebrew shebet (H7626) — rod, dart; 2 Samuel 18:14, three darts in the hand of Joab.
usage: “The shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts” — a soaked shield, raised beforehand.
“Three darts… thrust them through the heart of Absalom” — the rebellion ended.
“Till a dart strike through his liver” — Proverbs on the cost of the strange woman.

pos: n. (a standard, a signal; rendering Hebrew nes)
etymology: From Latin insignia, marks of distinction. An ensign is raised to be seen from far off — a rallying point rather than a weapon.
biblical_def: An ensign is a raised signal. Israel camped by them: “every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard, with the ensign of their father's house” (Num 2:2). Isaiah turns the word messianic: “in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek” (Isa 11:10), and again, “he will lift up an ensign to the nations from far” (Isa 5:26). The lifted signal gathers what was scattered.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ensign as the flag or banner of a military band; a banner of colors; a standard; and a signal to assemble or to give notice.
webster_full: ENSIGN, n. The flag or banner of a military band; a banner of colors; a standard; a figured cloth borne on a pole.
2. Any signal to assemble or to give notice.
3. A badge; a mark of distinction, rank or office.
scriptures: Num 2:2
Every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard, with the ensign of their father's house: far off about the tabernacle of the congregation shall they pitch.
And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek: and his rest shall be glorious.
Isa 5:26
And he will lift up an ensign to the nations from far, and will hiss unto them from the end of the earth: and, behold, they shall come with speed swiftly:
And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
corruption_summary: Churches raise ensigns constantly — brands, styles, causes — and gather people around them; Isaiah says only one lifted signal was ever meant to be the rallying point.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 11:10 makes the ensign a Person: there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek; and his rest shall be glorious. A standard works by being visible from a distance to people who cannot yet see each other, which is exactly how the gospel gathers strangers from every nation into one camp. What is raised determines who assembles.

Numbers 2 shows the ordinary use and its dignity. Every tribe camped by its own ensign in an assigned position around the tabernacle, so that the whole camp had order and every family knew where it belonged. Identity under a standard is not a modern anxiety; it is an ancient provision. The question Scripture presses is never whether a man will camp under a banner, only which one.
roots_summary: Hebrew nes (H5251), a standard, signal, pole — the same word in Jehovah-nissi, the LORD my banner (Exo 17:15).
roots_lines: Hebrew nes (H5251) — standard, ensign, signal; Isaiah 5:26, 11:10, 11:12, and Numbers 21:8 of the serpent set on a pole.
Hebrew degel (H1714) — banner, standard; Numbers 2:2, every man by his own standard.
Hebrew oth (H226) — sign, token; the ensign of their father's house.
usage: “Every man… shall pitch by his own standard” — order in the camp.
“A root of Jesse… shall stand for an ensign of the people” — the signal is a Person.
“He will lift up an ensign to the nations from far” — gathering what was scattered.

etymology: From Latin valere, to be strong. Valour is strength proved under fire — worth demonstrated rather than claimed.
biblical_def: Valour is proven courage. The phrase mighty man of valour is one of Scripture's standard commendations, and its most striking use is spoken over a man in hiding: the angel greets Gideon threshing wheat in a winepress with “The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour” (Jdg 6:12). Jephthah is introduced the same way despite his outcast origins (Jdg 11:1). The Hebrew chayil covers strength, ability, and substance — the same word rendered virtuous of the Proverbs 31 woman.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines valor as strength of mind in regard to danger; that quality which enables a man to encounter danger with firmness; personal bravery; courage; prowess.
webster_full: VALOR, n. Strength of mind in regard to danger; that quality which enables a man to encounter danger with firmness; personal bravery; courage; intrepidity; prowess.
scriptures: Jdg 6:12
And the angel of the LORD appeared unto him, and said unto him, The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour.
Jdg 11:1
Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty man of valour, and he was the son of an harlot: and Gilead begat Jephthah. Jephthah: called Jephte an

And of the Gadites there separated themselves unto David into the hold to the wilderness men of might, and men of war fit for the battle, that could handle shield and buckler, whose faces were like the faces of lions, and were as swift as the roes upon the mountains; of
Jdg 6:15
And he said unto him, Oh my Lord, wherewith shall I save Israel? behold, my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house. my
corruption_summary: Valour is assumed to describe men who already feel brave, when God's most famous use of the phrase is addressed to a frightened man hiding from his enemies.
corruption_paragraphs: Judges 6:12 is one of the great instances of God naming a man by what He intends to make him. Gideon is threshing wheat by a winepress to hide it from the Midianites — a picture of fear and reduced circumstances — and the greeting is thou mighty man of valour. His own reply is the opposite assessment: my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house. God's address is prophetic, not flattering.

The Hebrew chayil is worth carrying into the domestic sphere as well, since the same word describes the Proverbs 31 woman. Scripture does not maintain one vocabulary of strength for the battlefield and a weaker one for the household; the man of valour and the woman of valour are commended in identical terms, and both are measured by capability faithfully deployed rather than by temperament.
roots_summary: Hebrew chayil (H2428), strength, force, ability, wealth, an army — the same root behind virtuous in Proverbs 31:10.
roots_lines: Hebrew chayil (H2428) — valour, strength, substance; Judges 6:12, 11:1, 1 Chronicles 12:8.
Hebrew gibbor chayil — mighty man of valour; the standard commendation of a warrior.
Hebrew ishshah chayil — woman of valour; Proverbs 31:10, Ruth 3:11, the identical vocabulary.
usage: “The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour” — spoken to a man in hiding.
“I am the least in my father's house” — Gideon's own assessment.
“Men of might, and men of war fit for the battle” — David's gathered valour.

pos: n. pl. (sentries on the wall; rendering Hebrew tsaphah and shamar)
etymology: From watch, to keep awake. The watchman's whole office is wakefulness on behalf of sleepers.
biblical_def: Watchmen stand on the wall to warn. Ezekiel makes the office a picture of the prophet, with the blood-guilt spelled out: “if the watchman see the sword come, and blow not the trumpet, and the people be not warned… his blood will I require at the watchman's hand” (Eze 33:6). Isaiah rebukes watchmen who are blind, ignorant, and “loving to slumber” (Isa 56:10), and sets others on Jerusalem's walls who “shall never hold their peace day nor night” (Isa 62:6). The psalmist adds the limit of all watching: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain (Psa 127:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a watchman as a sentinel; a guard; one set to watch, especially in the night, for the security of a city or camp.
webster_full: WATCHMAN, n. A sentinel; a guard; one set to watch in the night.
2. One whose business is to guard against danger, and give notice of it.
scriptures: Eze 33:6

But if the watchman see the sword come, and blow not the trumpet, and the people be not warned; if the sword come, and take any person from among them, he is taken away in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at the watchman's hand.
His watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber.
Isa 62:6
I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem, which shall never hold their peace day nor night: ye that make mention of the LORD, keep not silence,
A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
corruption_summary: The watchman's office has been claimed by the perpetually alarmed, who blow the trumpet at everything, and abandoned by the comfortable, who blow it at nothing.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 33 sets terms that make the office serious in both directions. If the watchman warns and the people ignore him, he has delivered his soul; if he sees the sword and stays silent, the blood is required at his hand. The trumpet is not for the watchman's satisfaction but for the city's survival, which means a man who enjoys sounding it has misunderstood the job as thoroughly as the man who sleeps through it.

Isaiah 56:10 diagnoses the failure with unusual bite: his watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark. The image is of a guard dog that will not make noise — harmless, well-fed, and useless. Psalm 127:1 then keeps the whole office humble: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain. The wall is watched by men; it is kept by God.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsaphah (H6822), to look out, keep watch; shamar (H8104), to guard; shomer, a keeper — the same root as Cain's question about his brother.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsaphah (H6822) — to watch, look out; Ezekiel 3:17 and 33:2-7, I have set thee a watchman.
Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, guard; Psalm 127:1, Song 3:3, the watchmen that go about the city.
Greek gregoreo (G1127) — to be watchful; Mark 13:37, what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch.
usage: “His blood will I require at the watchman's hand” — silence has a price.
“Dumb dogs, they cannot bark” — the harmless, useless guard.
“Except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” — the limit of all vigilance.

pos: n. (a ditch, an entrenchment; rendering Hebrew tealah and maagalah)
etymology: From Old French trenchier, to cut. A trench is a cut in the ground — made for defence, for siege, or for water.
biblical_def: A trench is a cut ditch. Elijah's is the most famous: on Carmel he repaired the altar, laid the wood, and “made a trench about the altar, as great as would contain two measures of seed” (1Ki 18:32), then filled it with water three times so that the fire's work could not be mistaken. Saul sleeps in one while David steals his spear (1Sa 26:5–7). Christ foretold Jerusalem's siege in the same vocabulary: “thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round” (Luk 19:43).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a trench as a long narrow cut in the earth; a ditch; and in fortification, a deep ditch cut for defence or for approaching a besieged place.
webster_full: TRENCH, n. A long narrow cut in the earth; a ditch; as a trench for draining land.
2. In fortification, a deep ditch cut for defense, or to interrupt the approach of an enemy.
TRENCH, v.t. To cut or dig, as a ditch.
scriptures: And with the stones he built an altar in the name of the LORD: and he made a trench about the altar, as great as would contain two measures of seed.
Then the fire of the LORD fell, and consumed the burnt sacrifice, and the wood, and the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench.

And David arose, and came to the place where Saul had pitched: and David beheld the place where Saul lay, and Abner the son of Ner, the captain of his host: and Saul lay in the trench, and the people pitched round about him.
For the days shall come upon thee, that thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round, and keep thee in on every side,
corruption_summary: Christians look for ambiguous signs they can interpret generously, where Elijah engineered a test that would leave no room to explain the result away.
corruption_paragraphs: The trench on Carmel is a deliberate exclusion of every alternative explanation. Elijah could have simply prayed over dry wood; instead he dug a ditch, filled the trench with water, and drenched the sacrifice three times until the water ran round about the altar. When the fire fell it consumed the burnt sacrifice, the wood, the stones, the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench. The extra water existed so that no one present could file the event under coincidence.

There is a discipline in that for anyone praying about a decision. Vague requests produce vague answers that confirm whatever the asker already wanted; Elijah's method was to make the conditions so adverse that a positive result could only be attributed to God. Luke 19:43 shows the word's other edge — Christ weeping over a city whose enemies would cast a trench about her, because she knew not the time of her visitation.
roots_summary: Hebrew tealah (H8585), a conduit or trench; maagalah (H4570), an entrenchment or wagon-track; Greek charax (G5482), a palisade or siege-mound.
roots_lines: Hebrew tealah (H8585) — conduit, trench; 1 Kings 18:32, 35, 38.
Hebrew maagalah (H4570) — entrenchment, track; 1 Samuel 26:5, Saul lay in the trench.
Greek charax (G5482) — palisade, siege-work; Luke 19:43, thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee.
usage: “He made a trench about the altar” — a test built to exclude coincidence.
“Licked up the water that was in the trench” — the fire took even the obstacle.
“Thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee” — Christ weeping over the siege to come.

pos: n. (uproar, disorderly commotion; rendering Hebrew hamon, Greek thorubos)
etymology: From Latin tumultus, an uproar. A tumult is noise with a crowd in it — agitation that has stopped being individual.
biblical_def: A tumult is a crowd's uproar. The chief priests plan Christ's arrest around it — “not on the feast day, lest there be an uproar among the people” (Mat 26:5) — and Pilate yields when he “saw that he could prevail nothing, but that rather a tumult was made” (Mat 27:24). The psalmist locates its source and its Master: God “stilleth the noise of the seas, the noise of their waves, and the tumult of the people” (Psa 65:7), setting crowd-noise and ocean-noise in the same sentence as things only He quiets.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tumult as the commotion, disturbance or agitation of a multitude, usually accompanied with great noise, uproar and confusion of voices.
webster_full: TUMULT, n. The commotion, disturbance or agitation of a multitude, usually accompanied with great noise, uproar and confusion of voices.
2. Violent commotion or agitation with confusion of sounds.
3. Agitation; high excitement; irregular or confused motion.
scriptures: Mat 26:5
But they said, Not on the feast day, lest there be an uproar among the people.

When Pilate saw that he could prevail nothing, but that rather a tumult was made, he took water, and washed his hands before the multitude, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it.
Psa 65:7
Which stilleth the noise of the seas, the noise of their waves, and the tumult of the people.
And some cried one thing, some another, among the multitude: and when he could not know the certainty for the tumult, he commanded him to be carried into the castle.
corruption_summary: The crowd's roar is now manufactured on demand and mistaken for the voice of the people — and leaders, like Pilate, govern by measuring it.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 27:24 is the definitive account of leadership by tumult. Pilate saw that he could prevail nothing, but that rather a tumult was made, and he washed his hands and delivered an innocent man to be crucified. He had assessed the case correctly, said so publicly, and then made his decision on the basis of volume. Every leader who governs by the loudest available noise is standing in that basin, and the water has never yet cleaned anyone's hands.

Acts 21:34 supplies the comic detail that exposes what a tumult actually is: some cried one thing, some another, among the multitude; and when the chief captain could not know the certainty for the tumult, he commanded him to be carried into the castle. The crowd that nearly killed Paul could not have stated its own charge. Psalm 65:7 is the answer — the God who stills the sea's noise stills the people's, and He is not impressed by decibels.
roots_summary: Hebrew hamon (H1995), a multitude, roar; Greek thorubos (G2351), an uproar, tumult — used of both mourning crowds and riots.
roots_lines: Hebrew hamon (H1995) — multitude, noise, tumult; Psalm 65:7, Isaiah 17:12, the rushing of nations.
Greek thorubos (G2351) — uproar, tumult; Matthew 26:5, 27:24, Acts 21:34.
Greek stasis (G4714) — insurrection, dissension; Acts 19:40, in danger to be called in question for this day's uproar.
usage: “Lest there be an uproar among the people” — the arrest timed around the crowd.
“Rather a tumult was made” — Pilate governs by volume.
“He stilleth… the tumult of the people” — the sea and the mob quieted by one hand.
